sentences.text: Welcome back to the show.
Today I am talking to a founder who builds cameras in a garage.
How did this start?
We started in 2019 with three people and one soldering iron.
Nobody thought a garage team could ship a camera.
Okay.
The first prototype was heavy and the battery barely lasted a coffee break.
So what changed?
We threw away the case and started again from the sensor.
That was the hardest month of the whole project.
Why the sensor first?
Because everything else follows from it.
The lens, the heat, the size of the body.
Right.
Once the sensor was fixed, the case almost designed itself.
Let's talk about the number everyone quotes.
What did the second prototype do?
Our second prototype shot ninety minutes of four K on one charge, the longest in its class.
That is a big claim.
How did you measure it?
We ran it on a bench with a fan pointed at the sensor, then again without the fan.
Most teams would have stopped at the bench test.
Yeah.
You did not.
What did the field test look like?
So the second test was a week on a fishing boat in the rain.
A fishing boat.
That sounds miserable.
It was the week I almost quit, and I still think about it every morning.
But the camera came back working, and that changed everything.
What did the boat teach you about the design?
Salt gets everywhere.
Every seam, every button, every port needs a gasket.
Let's move to the team.
How do you hire for something this specialised?
Slowly.
We hire people who have shipped one hard thing, whatever it was.
That rules out most fresh graduates.
Mm-hm.
Does it?
Who was the best hire you made?
A retired watchmaker.
She taught us that tolerance is a habit, not a number.
I love that.
Let's talk about money.
Money was the boring part.
We sold prototypes to pay for the next one.
No investors at all?
Not until the boat test proved the design.
What is next for the camera?
A smaller body and a better screen.
The sensor stays.
So the hard part is done.
The hard part is never done.
It just moves.
Last question.
What would you tell someone starting in a garage today?
Ship one thing that works before you design the second thing.
That is a good place to end.
Thank you for coming.
Thank you for having me.
